paul_notes.doc: Paul's annotation file (sha12 4b53f8cc145e) is short: six cited works, each with a citation line and a commentary paragraph, and no reviewer comments. The annotation JSON at C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\4b53f8cc145e.json does not exist, so there are no comments or highlights to add. The file does not name Moneyball, Mentat, Terrier, or path-finding; the only system-facing language is "social network analysis vector graph" and "future allocation models". Taken together, the commentary argues four things. Lobbying pays: firms that lobby for beneficial legislation see large returns (Alexander), lobbying lifts revenue and concentration (Huneeus and Kim; Bickmore), with the revenue gain partly at the expense of the wider economy. Access and influence are bought through donations, and the effect is strongest for committee-related activity and fades unless renewed (Kim, In Song et al.). Information is filtered by staffers' ideology, so advocacy should be routed through ideologically aligned think tanks; Paul proposes treating think-tank funding like venture capital in allocation models. Existing position-mapping pipelines (Kim, Jiseon et al.) are useful for SNA but reactive and blind to inter-industry conflict over a bill, which Paul calls vital for political intelligence. The implied research questions are: does lobbying pay, and for whom (size, industry); do donations buy legislative involvement, and how durable is it; does the information source matter; and can position data be used predictively. Stated gaps: no predictive capability, no conflict detection, and no link yet from these findings to specific Melange, Moneyball, or Mentat components.

Quotes: several entries open with quoted findings from the papers. The anchors above are Paul's own commentary, not the quoted passages.

Overarching arguments: (1) lobbying yields large private returns, but partly at economy-wide misallocation cost; (2) influence is channelled through donations, and the effect is strongest for committee work and is time-limited without renewal; (3) staffers' ideological filtering shapes which information gets through, so advocacy should route through aligned think tanks; (4) current position-mapping pipelines are useful but reactive and miss inter-industry conflict.

Research questions implicit in the file: does lobbying pay, and does firm size or industry drive returns; do donations buy legislative involvement, and how long does it last; does the information source change receptivity; can position data be made predictive and conflict-aware.

Stated gaps: no predictive capability; no explicit conflict detection between industries over a bill; no explicit mapping from these findings to named Melange, Moneyball, Mentat or Terrier components. works.title: How Do Electoral Incentives Affect Legislator Behavior? Evidence from U.S. State Legislatures
works.summary:
Fouirnaies and Hall use term limits in 14 U.S. state legislatures (16 chambers, roughly 1991-2016) to ask whether reelection incentives change what legislators do. They compare each incumbent's binding final term with that same person's earlier terms, against same-chamber-year colleagues, using legislator and chamber-year fixed effects. In the final term, a PCA productivity index falls by 0.24 SD (N=11,109 legislator-terms). The drop ranges from -0.09 with seniority fixed effects to -0.41 with matched NY/TX controls. Roll-call participation falls 2.7 points from a mean of 90.5, bill sponsorship falls about 6% (-1.63 from a mean of 27.3 bills), and committee activity falls about 8%. Ideology does not move. |W-NOMINATE| changes by +0.02, the party-split estimates are about 0, and interest-group ratings across seven issue areas show no systematic shift. The authors read this as elections shaping visible effort, not positions. They add that legislators who leave to run for another office keep their electoral incentives, so the estimates are a lower bound.

For Paul's system, the paper matters in four places. (1) The receptivity layer cites it for a 0.60 "less responsive" multiplier on retiring members. The paper measured effort, not responsiveness to pressure. Its null on positions argues against reading the drop as movability, and its footnote 14 contradicts the retiring list, which includes members running for other office. (2) Several measures treat roll-call participation and sponsorship volume as dispositions or costly signals: diligence, the C criterion, the agenda volume and say-do path A. The paper shows these move with electoral status inside the same person. (3) The paper finds that effort and position separate cleanly, which supports keeping influence and alignment on separate axes. (4) Prospective test H2 cites this paper, but under it, retiring members' reduced activity can produce a correlation with no responsiveness behind it. The evidence comes from state legislatures with exogenous, binding limits. In Congress, retirement is voluntary and self-selected, so the effect transfers only weakly.
works.question: Do electoral incentives change how legislators allocate effort to visible activities (bill sponsorship, committee service, floor attendance), and do they change ideological positioning? The paper uses term limits as the source of variation in incentives.
works.method: OLS difference-in-differences at the individual level (eq. 3, p.669): Productivity_ict = beta * TermLimited_ict + alpha_i + delta_ct + eps_ict, with legislator fixed effects and chamber-year (or chamber-party-year) fixed effects; robust SEs clustered by legislator. Outcome is a PCA-based productivity index (first principal component of log bills sponsored, a committee activity index, and percent of floor votes cast; normalized mean 0, SD 1; p.667). Committee index weights: 0 non-member, 1 member, 2 vice chair, 3 chair, summed across committees (eq. 1-2, p.666). Ideology: W-NOMINATE first dimension, absolute value as extremity, and party-split W-NOMINATE (Table 5, p.673). Interest-group ratings (0-100) across abortion, business, education, environment, guns, taxes, labor unions and an "other" category, estimated with legislator-by-group and group-by-chamber-year fixed effects (eq. 4, p.672). Robustness: log seniority, seniority FE, cohort-year FE, and matched NY/TX synthetic controls with match-pair-year FE (Table 3, p.670).

findings.finding: Termed-out (final-term) legislators have lower legislative productivity index, the main outcome. The effect is about one-quarter SD and is unchanged with chamber-party-year FE.
findings.numbers: Term limited = -0.24 (SE 0.03) in both columns; N=11,109; 4,642 legislators; outcome SD 1.00

findings.finding: Effect is robust to alternative counterfactuals. It shrinks with seniority controls but stays negative and significant. It is larger with matched NY/TX controls, which address both learning and anticipation.
findings.numbers: Log(seniority) -0.23 (SE 0.03); seniority FE -0.09 (0.03); cohort-year FE -0.09 (0.03); matched NY/TX -0.41 (0.03), N=11,416, 1,506 legislators

findings.finding: Floor attendance falls in the final term. Abstention rises from about 10% to 12.7% of votes, a proportional increase of about 27%. The authors say the effect is meaningfully larger than the term-length effect in Titiunik (2016).
findings.numbers: Percentage of floor votes = -2.70 (SE 0.53); -2.63 with party-year FE; outcome mean 90.48

findings.finding: Bill sponsorship falls in the final term, about 6% in proportional terms.
findings.numbers: Sponsored bills = -1.63 (SE 0.77) and -1.34 (SE 0.70) against mean 27.32; N=16,727; 6,207 legislators

findings.finding: Committee activity falls in the final term, about 8% in proportional terms.
findings.numbers: Committee activity = -0.31 (SE 0.06) and -0.30 (SE 0.05) against mean 3.84; N=16,255; 6,123 legislators

findings.finding: Heterogeneity fits theory. Effects are larger under lifetime limits than consecutive limits, in more professionalized legislatures, and where salaries are higher. Effects are also larger in California and Oklahoma, where limits are cumulative.
findings.location: Appendix Table A.3, summarized in text p.671 (table not in extracted text)
findings.numbers: No numeric values in main text

related.why: Fouirnaies & Hall rely on individual-level two-way fixed-effects DiD with a staggered final-term treatment and admit they cannot run pretrend tests (p.669). Imai & Kim's critique of TWFE causal assumptions applies directly when judging how far the -0.24 SD estimate should transfer.

Ramey links text-measured Conscientiousness to bill-sponsorship behavior (a lower share of ceremonial bills, Table 3). Fouirnaies & Hall show sponsorship and participation also move with electoral incentive inside the same person, a situational confound for any trait reading of those behaviours (diligence_z, the C criterion).

The two are sibling factors in the receptivity layer: Fouirnaies & Hall drive incent_mult 0.60 and Linde & Vis drive pt_mult. Both condition on electoral situation, and the code notes they share an input (security drives both incent and pt).

Both papers study U.S. state legislatures. Bucchianeri's state-level effectiveness scores are the outcome-side counterpart to Fouirnaies & Hall's effort index, and would show whether final-term effort losses reduce effectiveness.

Fouirnaies & Hall's ideology null rests on W-NOMINATE scaling of state roll calls, from the NOMINATE family Poole reviews. The paper itself states the scaling may be too coarse to detect issue-specific shifts (p.668, p.673).

works.title: Legislative Effectiveness in the American States
works.summary:
Bucchianeri, Volden and Wiseman adapt the congressional Legislative Effectiveness Score to state legislatures. The result is the SLES: 80,344 legislator-term scores across 97 chambers, 1987-2018, built from about 1.8 million bills. Each score is a weighted average of 15 indicators: the share of a member's sponsored bills that reach each of five stages (introduced, action in committee, action beyond committee, passed chamber, law), at three significance levels weighted 1, 5 and 10. Scores are normalized to mean 1 within each chamber-term. The authors stress that absolute scores should not be compared across chambers or eras.

They check validity three ways. A hand audit found 95.2% of 49,037 sampled bills correctly coded. In North Carolina (2005-2012), SLES alone explains about half the variance in subjective effectiveness rankings and beats simple hit rates. Scores also persist from term to term (rho 0.38-0.66, highest when majority control does not change). In pooled OLS, majority status adds 0.370 (0.362 lower chamber, 0.387 upper) and a committee chair adds 0.507 (0.609 lower vs 0.307 upper). Moderates are more effective. Two exploratory chamber-level studies find that majority advantage grows with polarization, majority-party cohesion and professionalism. All results are associational.

What this means for Paul's system: the paper is the direct method source for the unactivated effectiveness shadow (fec/engine/legislative_effectiveness.py), which copies the five stages, the 1/5/10 weights and per-chamber-term normalization. The shadow departs from SLES in two ways: it credits cosponsors, and it measures significance by CU mention frequency. The paper's validation evidence therefore does not carry over to those changes. The paper also exposes three weak spots in the live rank:
- Leg% and Influence% are pooled across the House and Senate.
- The efficiency term is the hit-rate kind of measure the paper outperforms.
- Nothing controls for majority status, which the paper finds is the largest structural driver of advancement.

The brain already records that CEL LES is roughly orthogonal to the live score (+0.10 Spearman).
works.question: Can individual state legislators' lawmaking effectiveness be measured comparably across 97 state legislative chambers and over time, and does the measure validly capture effectiveness? Two illustrative questions follow: (1) how does the majority-party advantage in lawmaking vary with ideological polarization, majority-party cohesion, and seat-share imbalance? (2) how do institutional designs (pay, professionalism, session length, staff, agenda-control and gatekeeping rules, committee-appointment votes, chamber size, term limits) shape the relative lawmaking power of majority vs minority, chairs vs rank-and-file, and senior vs freshman legislators? (pp. 21-22, 30-34)
works.method:
Measure: a weighted average of 15 indicators. These are the shares of a legislator's bills that reach each of five stages (introduced, action in committee, action beyond committee, passed home chamber, became law) at each of three significance levels (commemorative weight 1, substantive weight 5, substantive and significant weight 10). Scores are normalized so each chamber-term has mean 1 (Eq. 1, pp. 23-24). Validity checks: hand-coding audit, North Carolina criterion validation, and construct validation via lagged correlations and OLS. Table 1 is OLS with fixed effects by term and chamber (or state), with standard errors clustered by legislator. Tables 2 and 3 are chamber-level OLS with standard errors clustered by state chamber. Outcomes are the median majority-minus-minority SLES gap, the share of majority members above the minority median, and median differences for chairs vs rank-and-file and non-freshmen vs freshmen. Tests are two-tailed (+p<0.1, *p<0.05, **p<0.01).</method>
<parameter name="identification">No causal identification strategy. Results are associational. Fixed effects absorb state, chamber and term differences. The authors state that endogeneity is unaddressed: rules may be chosen by strong parties, and term limits or professionalism may respond to entrenched power (p. 34). Study 2 is framed as illustrative and exploratory.

findings.finding: Hand-coding audit of the bill-coding pipeline: research assistants found 46,693 of 49,037 sampled bills (95.2%) accurately coded; after fixes, alignment exceeded 99%.
Criterion validity: SLES tracks North Carolina's subjective NCCPPR effectiveness rankings and outperforms hit-rate metrics.
findings.location: p. 24; Figure 1; Table A4 in Supplementary Appendix
findings.numbers: SLES alone explains about half the variance in NCCPPR rankings (2005-2012)

findings.finding: Construct validity over time: lagged SLES correlates positively with current SLES, strongest when majority control is unchanged.
findings.numbers: rho = 0.38 (entered majority), 0.40 (entered minority), 0.66 (no change in control)

findings.finding: Seniority, chairs, and majority status predict higher SLES in the pooled OLS (Model 1.1).
findings.numbers: Seniority 0.032 per term (about 3% of mean 1); Committee chair 0.507; Majority party 0.370, which is 58% above the minority mean of 0.636 (p. 26)

findings.finding: Ideological moderates are more effective (distance from chamber median is negative), and women and African American and Hispanic legislators score lower on average.
findings.numbers: Distance from Median -0.114 (p<0.01); Female -0.034 (p<0.05) in full sample; African American -0.101 (p<0.01); Hispanic -0.078 (p<0.01)

findings.finding: Institutional positions matter more in lower chambers; the Table 1 advantages of leadership, chairs and power committees are larger in the lower chamber.
findings.numbers: Committee chair 0.609 (lower) vs 0.307 (upper); Majority party 0.362 vs 0.387 (similar)

related.why: Both are measures of which legislators get bills advanced. This paper does not cite Sotoudeh, so the link is the analyst's inference, not a citation.
Both study US state legislators using state bill-sponsorship records. The paper does not cite Fouirnaies and Hall, so the same-data label is downgraded to complements.
